11179-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Edited by Francis W. Halsey, this sixth volume of a travel anthology gathers famous writers describing Hungary, Austria's Adriatic ports, and the Alps. Readers move from Hungarian baths and gipsy camps to Trieste, Spalato, Ragusa, and Cattaro, then into the Tyrol, the Dolomites, and Swiss resorts such as Interlaken, Lucerne, and Zermatt. A final section follows early Alpine climbers up the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc.

Each stop comes in a different author's voice, from Bayard Taylor on the road to Prague to Shelley on a Chamonix avalanche. The collection works as armchair travel and as a record of how English-speaking travelers saw central Europe before modern tourism. Its variety is its strength: no single guide, but many witnesses.
12236-death-valley-in-49-important-chapt:
William Lewis Manly published Death Valley in 49 in 1894, an autobiography of a pioneer who traveled from a humble Green Mountain home to the California gold mines. Manly tells the story of the band of men, women, and children who gave Death Valley its name.

The narrative follows overland travel, thirst, and confusion in the desert, with passages on dreadful sands, salty columns, bitter lakes, and sunken desolation. Manly writes of phantoms born of exhaustion and of the hope that sea waves might one day cover the barren waste. The book is a first-hand account of the 1849 emigration at its worst. Its plain style and terrible detail made it a classic of California pioneer history.
12404-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, volume five, covers Germany and parts of Austria-Hungary, with a note that part two, volume six, is a separate text. The series lets readers tour Europe through the eyes of famous writers.

Selections describe Berlin, the Rhine, and Austrian towns, with a mid-book passage on Berlin drawn from Hoffmann fantastic stories: a strange, grotesque city peopled with aulic councillors, sandmen, Kreislers, and archivist Lindursts. The volume pairs travel description with literary association, so a street recalls a tale. It suits armchair travelers and students who want Europe through books, not guidebooks alone.
15176-english-literature-considered-as-a:
Henry Coppée, president of Lehigh University, wrote this 1873 manual to teach English history through English literature. He argues that a nation's ideas, shown in its books, reveal its history as surely as events do. A Merivale motto on the Roman epic opens the case for reading literature as a record of mind.

Chapters move through periods and authors, using poems, plays, and prose to light up the age that made them. Coppée writes for students and teachers who want history with a human voice. The book remains a thoughtful, if dated, guide to reading literature as history.
16259-the-surprising-adventures-of-the-m:
L. Frank Baum's Surprising Adventures of the Magical Monarch of Mo and His People, published in 1903 with pictures by Frank Ver Beck, offers children pure nonsense joy. Baum tells readers he has no shame in admitting he is also a child, since his eyes still grow big at marvels and his heart still beats fast at impossible adventures. Childhood, he says, is the time for fables, dreams, and joy, before realities crowd in.

Ten surprises follow in the book. The beautiful valley of Mo and the king's head come first. Then come the tramp dog, fruit cake island, and a birthday. King Scowleyow's cast-iron man, Timtom and Princess Pattycake, and Prince Jollikin's bravery follow. Baum warns that the tales are not true, only meant to excite laughter. Young readers will find a delightful Oz-era fantasy.
16919-the-bradys-and-the-girl-smuggler-o:
A New York detective wrote this July 27, 1900 dime novel, number 79 of Secret Service. Old and Young King Brady Detectives lead the series, issued weekly by Frank Tousey in New York for five cents. It opens with the Collector of the Port scolding his chief inspectors in the Custom House. Then Old King Brady brings a warrant for a lady's daughter on a charge of smuggling. Harry lets a hall boy go as the scene unfolds.

The Bradys work for the Custom House, chasing smugglers through New York's docks and drawing rooms. The tale moves fast, with arrests, disguises, and narrow escapes in short chapters. Readers who like old dime novels will find a brisk, plot-first adventure, full of period slang and the bustle of a port city.
17185-stories-about-the-instinct-of-anim:
Thomas Bingley's 1851 book, with engravings after T. Landseer, has Uncle Thomas tell children about animal instinct, character, and habits. The horse opens the set: great herds on South American plains, lasso capture, an Arab and his mare, and tales of horse sense, love, and docility. Beavers and their dams, sociable grosbeaks, white ants of Africa, and elephants caught wild follow.

Uncle Thomas speaks in a kind, instructive voice, mixing wonder with moral lessons for young listeners. The book suits children and animal lovers who like old-style nature tales. Its charm lies in short, vivid stories that show beasts as clever, loyal, and worthy of kind care.
19342-complete-hypnotism-mesmerism-mind-:
A. Alpheus wrote this 1903 manual, Complete Hypnotism, Mesmerism, Mind-Reading and Spiritualism, promising an exhaustive, practical system of method and use. Chapters teach how to hypnotise by the methods of Cocke, Flint, Paris, Nancy, and the Hindoo silent method, how to wake subjects, and how to spot frauds in stage shows.

Later chapters cover amusing trials, a whip turned to hot iron, courting a broomstick, stages from lethargy to somnambulism, self-hypnosis, and the history from Mesmer and Puysegur onward. Readers get a period guide to hypnotism, curious, confident, and best read as history, not as medical advice.
19811-a-book-of-english-prose-part-ii-ar:
A Book of English Prose, Part Two, was arranged for secondary and high schools. Its selections reach back to Malory's King Arthur tales. One passage brings Arthur home by sea to Dover. Sir Mordred waits there with his host to block the landing. Father and son meet as enemies on the shore. The prose is Malory's, in schoolroom dress.

School anthologies built a shared literary memory. Students met Arthur, and much else, through such excerpts. Editors chose passages that modeled strong English prose. Part two implies a graded course across school years. The Malory sample shows history, legend, and style at once. Books like this decided what 'English prose' meant to pupils.
27748-popular-lectures-on-zoonomia-or-th:
Thomas Garnett's popular lectures on zoonomia, the laws of animal life in health and disease, were published in 1804 for the benefit of his orphan children. Garnett, the Royal Institution's first lecturer, had died before the volume appeared.

The lectures open with a life of the author, then explain bones, muscles, nerves, and senses before turning to respiration and other bodily functions. Written for general listeners, they show early nineteenth-century medicine trying to make the workings of the body clear to non-specialists. Garnett had been professor of natural philosophy and chemistry at the Royal Institution.
31829-a-translation-of-the-new-testament:
T. Haweis's 1795 translation of the New Testament from the original Greek, printed in London for T. Chapman, was humbly attempted to assist the unlearned with clearer and more explicit views of the mind of the Spirit in the scriptures of truth. Haweis, rector of All-Saints, Aldwinckle, and chaplain to the late Countess of Huntingdon, invites learned brethren to point out his mistakes for correction.

He respects the Reformers' translation, whose language has dignity, but argues that the present version holds obscurities, obsolete words, and feeble expressions for which more accurate ones may be substituted. Readers get an eighteenth-century New Testament in plain English, made for men of common capacity without Greek.
32456-r-e-h:
R. H. Barlow's sonnet, printed in Weird Tales in October 1936, mourns Robert E. Howard, creator of Conan, who died June 11, 1936. Barlow pictures Conan, the warrior king, lying stricken dead beneath a sky of cryptic stars, his laughter stilled like a lute, his youthful head resting on chilling earth. No clamorous fray sounds for him now, only dirges where trumpets once rang, with old memories pressing around him for a shroud.

Death, Barlow writes, spilled the blood of a man who loved battle the way men love mistresses, and fought it well. His young flesh lies like marble where he fell, his sword broken, having vanquished all but Night. Barlow closes by placing Conan among mythic kings, roaming where dreamers seek, a fitting farewell from one fantasy writer to another.
32601-legends-of-ma-ui-a-demi-god-of-pol:
W. D. Westervelt's Legends of Ma-ui, published in Honolulu in 1910, retells Polynesian stories of Maui, a demi-god, and his mother Hina. Four brothers bear the name Maui. The youngest leads the tales, waking his brothers with unexpected tricks and drawing them into feats across Hawaii, Tonga, Tahiti, New Zealand, and the Hervey group.

Chapters follow Maui the fisherman, lifting the sky, snaring the sun, finding fire, and seeking immortality, alongside Hina of Hilo, Hina and the Wailuku River, and Hina, the woman in the moon. Westervelt adds pronunciation help, treating Maui as both supernatural and very human, scolded at home yet endowed with magic.
32813-the-wives-of-henry-the-eighth-and-:
Martin Hume follows the six wives of Henry VIII through the politics they shaped, in a London volume from Eveleigh Nash dated 1905. Nine chapters run from 1488 to 1547, opening with why Katharine of Aragon came to England. Portraits face the text, including Holbein portraits of Katharine and Jane Seymour.

Hume treats each marriage as political matrimony first and personal drama second. Katharine's widowhood, the divorce struggle, and Anne Boleyn's fleeting triumph each get a chapter. Jane Seymour and Anne of Cleves share a chapter of plot and counterplot. The book closes with Katharine Howard, Katharine Parr, and the Protestants winning the last trick.
33596-mary-help-of-christians-and-the-fo:
The Reverend Bonaventure Hammer compiled this Catholic devotional, published by Benziger Brothers in 1909 with imprimatur (church license) from the Archbishop of New York. It offers instructions, legends, novenas, and prayers for Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints invoked as Holy Helpers, together with thoughts of the saints for every day of the year. An appendix by the Reverend John J. Burke treats the reasonableness of Catholic ceremonies and practices.

Part One explains the veneration (deep respect) and invocation (calling for help) of saints, the efficacy (true power) of their intercession (prayers for others), and the qualities of prayer. Part Two gives novenas for the principal feasts of the Blessed Virgin, with rules for observing them and meditations for each day. The volume is a thorough manual of traditional Catholic devotion, still useful to readers exploring that spiritual practice.
34214-francis-beaumont-dramatist-a-portr:
Charles Mills Gayley's 1914 study Francis Beaumont: Dramatist paints the life of the Elizabethan and Jacobean playwright and his circle. Part one follows Beaumont from Grace-Dieu and Oxford to the Inns of Court, the stage, marriage, and death.

Part two takes up the hard puzzle of his work with John Fletcher: which plays each man wrote, and how their joint voice came to be. Gayley also sets Beaumont among Shakespeare, Jonson, and the Gunpowder Plot circle of his Vaux kin, giving a full portrait of a life in a crowded age. Gayley wrote as professor of English at the University of California.
6816-canadian-wild-flowers-selections-fr:
Helen Johnson of Magog, Quebec, speaks in Canadian Wild Flowers through selections from her writings, with a sketch of her life by J. M. Orrock. Good thoughts, a verse says, spring from the human mind like flowers from the ground, attractive, fragrant, and lovely, to make joys abound. More than twenty years after Johnson's death, her name still smells like ointment poured forth.

Readers who never knew her feel they know her well from her poems, fragrant as flowers to the sense. Orrock's preface ties her verse to God's providence and to the written word. Canadian Wild Flowers is a tender, pious memorial to a beloved Canadian poet.
canadian-wild-flowers-selections-from-th:
Canadian Wild Flowers gathers selections from the writings of Helen M. Johnson of Magog, Quebec, with Rev. J. M. Orrock's sketch of her life. Johnson died more than twenty years before the book appeared, yet her name remained, in the preface's phrase, like an ointment poured forth.

The selections present Johnson's poems and reflections on nature, faith and providence, showing why readers who never knew her felt they knew her well. Her verse treats wild flowers as emblems of good thoughts springing from the human mind, attractive, fragrant and beautiful. The volume suits readers of Canadian poetry and of Victorian devotional verse, offering a gentle introduction to a little-known writer.
complete-hypnotism-mesmerism-mind-readin:
Complete Hypnotism, Mesmerism, Mind-Reading and Spiritualism, by A. Alpheus, promises an exhaustive and practical system of method, application, and use. Its chapters teach stage work first: amusing experiments, post-hypnotic suggestion, a whip turned to hot iron in a subject's hands, and the courting of a broomstick. The stages of hypnotism follow: lethargy, catalepsy, the somnambulistic stage, and fascination.

An introduction gives the art an ancient pedigree: the mysteries of Isis, laying on of hands, the trances of Delphi, and the fakirs of India. Later chapters turn critical. Simulation and fraud in hypnotism are exposed, criminal suggestion is debated and doubted, and the dangers of public performances are condemned. Medical uses, animal hypnotism, and telepathy close the course.
death-valley-in-49-important-chapter-of-:
An autobiography of a California pioneer fills William Lewis Manly's book of 1894, entered at the Library of Congress that year. Manly inscribes it to the pioneers of California and their children and grandchildren. His road runs from a humble home in the Green Mountains of Vermont to the gold mines.

Early chapters tell of the western fever, the Erie Canal, deer killing, and fever and ague in Michigan. Then comes the gold news and the long trek. The heart of the book is the suffering of the party of men, women, and children who gave Death Valley its name. Manly calls the valley a sunken desolation of salt and bitter lakes, with naught of good in it. The book is a first-hand record of 1849.
doe-osti-1415858-tethered-balloon-system:
A balloon system that carries instruments on a tether fills this handbook, numbered DOE/SC-ARM-TR-206 and dated February 2026. D Dexheimer of Sandia National Laboratories leads the authors. Z Cheng, K Gaustad, and F Mei of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, J Creamean of Colorado State University, and J Sammon and C Longbottom of Sandia join the byline.

The system flies with a pressure sensor about one metre above the surface, the text notes. A ceilometer usually works beside it, giving cloud base and mixing layer heights, though it runs apart from the balloon ground station. A Doppler lidar near the site is likewise run on its own. The handbook sets out the parts, the flights, and the data for users of the facility.
doe-osti-17049046-computational-modeling:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-25/51 models how much water road drainage hardware can take in when water ponds around it, a state called sump conditions. Marta Sitek and Steven Lottes studied South Carolina Department of Transportation catch basins and drop inlets with fluid flow simulation. Such ratings guide road design and flood control.

The model includes pavement roughness and vegetation effects on flow. Two catch basins, CB 9 and CB 18, and three drop inlets, including a 24 by 36 inch unit, each get a full capacity chapter. Tabulated capacity data in an appendix are formatted for use as inputs to a spreadsheet design aid for engineers.
doe-osti-2574213-development-of-li-s-bat:
Final scientific and technical report DE-EE0009650, from Pennsylvania State University under Daiwei Wang and covering October 2021 to March 2025, develops lithium-sulfur battery cells for electric vehicles. Sulfur promises up to three times the energy density of today's lithium-ion cathodes, at roughly a hundredth of the material cost of cobalt oxide. Three flaws block the market: sulfur insulates, its discharge products dissolve and wander, and lithium dendrites grow on the anode.

The team's answer is a cathode material that never forms soluble polysulfides, the wandering species, while still holding more than fifty percent sulfur by weight. Earlier polysulfide-free cathodes carried too little sulfur and reacted sluggishly. The new cathodes were paired with functional binders, tuned electrolyte mixes, and refined electrode fabrication. The report presents cells combining high energy density with long cycle life, and judges the design a real step toward practical, low-cost lithium-sulfur batteries.
doe-osti-2575489-theory-and-user-manual-:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-25/44, by Zhaopeng Zhong and Micheal A. Smith, finally documents a code that ran for decades without a manual. SE2-ANL is a special version of SUPERENERGY-2, a steady-state thermal hydraulics code for liquid metal reactor cores. It was developed in the 1980s to compute temperatures across many fuel assemblies at once, and no complete documentation was ever written until now.

The manual explains the temperature calculation method inherited from the original code, then the fuel and cladding temperature capabilities added in the ANL version. Geometry and noding generation, heat transfer between assemblies, and facial boundary conditions each get a section. Features such as the orificing zone option, which balances coolant flow among assemblies, are described in working detail. Input and output are demonstrated on simple models, so new users can reproduce results instead of reverse-engineering old input decks.
doe-osti-3003001-past-approaches-for-spe:
Rob P. Rechard reviews four decades of American nuclear waste policy in Sandia report SAND2025-13802, printed October 2025. This is part one of a two-part history. It covers spent nuclear fuel, high-level waste, and transuranic waste bound for deep geologic disposal. Its focus is safety criteria: how regulators set the standards a repository must meet, and how they treat uncertainty in forecasts that run thousands of years.

The narrative runs through the Nuclear Waste Policy Act and the Environmental Protection Agency standards applied at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico. International experts working with the IAEA informed the account. Rechard writes as an insider-historian of the programs he evaluates. Readers weighing a future repository effort get the regulatory record in one place, including how proof of safety was argued.
doe-osti-3008368-summary-of-analytical-s:
Analytical services behind the Hanford Site radionuclide air program are summed up in document HNF-61951, Revision 6, by D. L. Dyekman of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions, dated November 2025. The program follows the federal NESHAP standard, which caps radioactive emissions from stacks and vents.

The summary sets contract detection limits, assigns sample location codes to facilities across the 200 East and 200 West areas, and estimates the 2026 workload in a collection table. Stack tables pair each emission unit with the analyses its samples receive, down to isotopes such as plutonium-238 and americium-241. Labs use the document to plan sampling and analysis for compliance.
doe-osti-3010315-automatic-generation-of:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0022223, by Martin Burtscher with Sheng Di and Franck Cappello, presents the LC framework, software that writes its own data compressors. Scientific instruments and exascale computers produce data faster than it can be stored, so compression must be both fast and trustworthy.

LC synthesizes millions of candidate algorithms and searches for the best fit to a given dataset, emitting parallel CPU and GPU versions with bit-identical output. Its lossy compressors guarantee the user's error bound. One generated compressor, SPspeed, compressed 75 times faster and decompressed 55 times faster than FPzip, the ratio leader. The framework and a tutorial are freely available on GitHub.
doe-osti-3014224-advanced-pem-electrolyz:
Plug Power's final report for award DE-EE0011328, led by Fan Yang with Qiang Sun, covers September 2024 to August 2025 and attacks hydrogen crossover in PEM electrolyzers. In these machines, some hydrogen leaks through the membrane into the oxygen side, wasting product and creating a safety risk that blocks high-pressure operation. Thick membranes slow the leak but waste energy through resistance.

With Ionomr Innovations, Washington University in St. Louis, and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, the team developed hydrocarbon membranes carrying a gas recombination catalyst that converts stray hydrogen back before it accumulates. Partner labs synthesized platinum nanoparticles by a surfactant-free route in ethylene glycol at 130 degrees Celsius for four hours, a method chosen for scale-up. The design aims to allow thinner, more efficient membranes without the crossover penalty.
doe-osti-3023223-chemical-recycling-of-p:
Massimiliano Delferro and Robert M Kennedy of Argonne National Laboratory close a cooperative project on turning plastic waste into higher value lubricants, in final CRADA report ANL/CSE-CP2022-22111. Chemical recycling breaks long plastic chains down with catalysts instead of heat alone. The product here is not fuel but wax and lubricant-grade material, which sells for more.

The team made platinum nanoparticles on a strontium titanate support, first activating the surface to raise hydroxyl density, then depositing the metal by surface organometallic chemistry and reducing it under hydrogen. Batch hydrogenolysis of polymer scaled from 3 grams to 25 grams. Conversion proved mass-transfer limited, so reaction time rose from 48 hours to 144 hours for the larger batches, and the high-melt wax was then solvent-washed and melt-treated.
doe-osti-3023417-energy-storage-and-the-:
Jeremy B Twitchell, Devyn W Powell, Krissy J Govertsen, and Jess B Kincaid of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory ask how energy storage can make electricity more affordable, in a March 2026 report. Their title invokes the law of averages: storage smooths the peaks and valleys of demand and renewable output. When a system is run closer to its average, less idle capacity has to be paid for.

One example pairs storage with conservation voltage reduction, where a utility trims voltage slightly to save energy. A little storage adds flexibility to such programs, and the report cites cases where savings more than offset the storage cost, lowering total operating cost. Storage also helps hold distribution voltage within required ranges and can strengthen demand response and other advanced management techniques.
doe-osti-3028343-stability-augmented-opt:
Jin Tan of the National Laboratory of the Rockies leads a large nine-partner team on the SAPPHIRE project, reported in NLR/TP-5D00-96932, dated April 2026. SAPPHIRE tackles stability and optimal control for hybrid photovoltaic plants where inverter-based resources reach very high penetration. Partners include the University of Tennessee, Purdue, Mississippi State, Kauai's utility cooperative, Hawaiian Electric, Hitachi Energy, and the Electric Power Research Institute.

Hawaiian island grids, already rich in inverters, supply the test events. Figures estimate rate of change of frequency over 0.05 second windows during arresting and transient events. One section builds inertia estimation from ambient data, since classic methods wait for ringdown events that do not happen daily and give only coarse answers. Ambient estimates can run often enough for real-time scheduling, which is what an inverter-heavy grid needs.
doe-osti-3375092-molecular-dynamics-simu: Los Alamos National Laboratory poster LA-UR-26-25147, issued June 22, 2026, by Cesar A. López Bautista, Sang-Min Shin, and Ramesh K. Jha, reports simulation checks on an engineered FAST protein. Its panels plot residue motion, scored as RMSF, for protein variants at 25 and 95 degrees Celsius. Labels mark mutations such as Q41R and A44K, and one variant carries the tag w25_proteng. The plots support the title claim, that hydrogen bonds hold the engineered protein steady under heat.
doe-osti-3376462-a-comprehensive-compari:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4669, dated June 2026, compares the world's main building height data sets against each other. Justin Epting heads the printed team. Clinton Stipek and Andrew Reith of the lab follow, with George Mason University among the partners. Height maps feed flood models, energy studies, and disaster plans. Each maker builds its map a different way, so the maps often disagree on the same street.

The team lined the products up at two scales. One is a grid of one hundred meter cells. The other is the single building. Twenty cities anchor the test: five with trusted reference data, fifteen without. Several scoring methods then rank each product per city. The design shows where a map is safe to use and where it drifts, a guide for buyers who now pick on faith.
doe-osti-3625677-development-and-validat:
Report NLR/TP-5K00-101001, dated August 2026, closes a SIPS project on low-cost mirror facets for concentrating solar power. Six authors are printed: Matthew Muller, Devon Kesseli, and Heyaw Getabecha of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, plus Saeed Farahani, Daniel Brown, and Jatin Vinay Badkar of Clemson University. The facets are sandwich panels meant to reflect sunlight well while costing less than glass mirrors.

Tests covered full one-metre square facets, small bend samples, hail hits, and heat and damp exposure. One core foam cracked and shrank in a hot, damp chamber, so the test heat was lowered for later runs. A switch to deionized water in the large chamber stopped the corrosion seen on galvanized sheets. Sections close with lessons on making the panels, on mirror surface decay, and on package strength. The work points to where the design still needs care before field use.
english-literature-considered-as-an-inte:
Henry Coppée reads England's past through its poems and plays in English Literature, Considered as an Interpreter of English History, a manual of instruction in its second edition of 1873. Coppée, president of Lehigh University, dedicates the book to Bishop William Bacon Stevens, his friend of forty years. His epigraph, from Merivale, calls national literature the most precious document of national history.

Chapters pair literary ages with the events behind them, from the Saxons and Danes to the Norman Conquest and beyond. Political poems get weighed as evidence: one paper of Prior's, he notes, won its author a commissionership. Coppée writes for students, summarizing the idea that a nation's mind shows in its books. The manual served classrooms that taught literature and history as one subject.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BarkerWilliamH_:
William W. Barker Jr. of New Orleans went to the FBI with a complaint, and the Bureau recorded it on form TD-71. The complaint named Lee Harvey Oswald, among others, as a subject, placing Barker's claims in the Bureau's own paperwork.

Complaint forms were the intake valve of the Bureau: any citizen's suspicion could become a file, to be checked or filed away. After the assassination, thousands of such reports about Oswald and his New Orleans summer were logged and chased down. This form is preserved as filed, a page of the intake record behind the investigation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CooperWilliamH_: An internal FBI memorandum dated March 15, 1967 was sent by Mr. Rosen and circulated to Cartha DeLoach and other senior Bureau officials. Only a fragment survives, and its subject cannot be recovered from what remains. What the record does preserve is the routing itself: who wrote the memo, who received it, and the date it moved through FBI headquarters.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISellingAlanH:
A San Francisco Chronicle clipping dated September 14, 1976 tells an informant's story. Alan H. Selling said his FBI contacts directed him to enter an attorney's home illegally. The goal was information on a Weather Underground fugitive the Bureau was hunting.

An informant accusing his own handlers of ordering a break-in put the Bureau in a hard light. The Weather Underground hunt had already raised questions about illegal searches. Selling's account, printed in a major paper, added a named voice to those charges. The clipping preserves his version as readers first saw it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LattaJohnH_Latt:
An unnamed writer complained to Harold Weisberg that a mailed letter had arrived with its envelope torn open. The writer blamed postal inspectors for snooping in the mail. The same file also contains an appended rant about Oklahoma City, attached to the complaint. The sender never names himself in the text.

Mail tampering was a live fear among assassination researchers. They traded documents by post and suspected official eyes on their work. Whether or not inspectors opened this envelope, the letter records that suspicion plainly. It also shows how unrelated grievances could end up filed together in a researcher's papers, kept because they arrived together.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LindsayWilliamH:
Harold Weisberg interviewed William Lindsay on November 5, 1968, and wrote up the talk the next day in a memo to Andrew Sciambra. Sciambra worked with the New Orleans district attorney's office on the Kennedy case. Lindsay told Weisberg he knew little about Clay Shaw. Years earlier, he said, he had only acted as a broker on some properties.

Shaw was then awaiting trial on the charge of conspiring to kill President Kennedy. Researchers chased anyone who had dealt with him, hoping for a link. Lindsay's interview is a record of a lead that led nowhere: a man questioned because of an old business contact, who had nothing more to give.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewtonAlexander: Filed under Alexander HNewton, this declassified US government document comes via the Internet Archive. The catalog is silent on date, agency, and matter - the name is all we have. No public text located. A placeholder record for the name.
govdocs-archive_org-the-history-of-the-h: Lev N. Gumilev wrote a history of the Hunnu nation, the nomadic people known in European tradition as the Huns. Gumilev, a Soviet ethnographer, studied the steppe peoples of Central Asia across long spans of time. His account follows the Hunnu as they built a steppe empire and dealt with China and the West. The volume serves readers of nomad history and of Gumilev's bold theories about peoples and their energy.
nasa-tm-19670024079-survival-of-selected:
Jean W. Mardres, of the Space Biology Branch at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this study in December 1966. It tests how selected microorganisms survive a high ultraviolet flux. The catalog record says the exposure matched the ultraviolet conditions on the surface of Mars. The work formed early groundwork for planetary exploration and protection.

The report is organized as a laboratory exposure study. Opening sections set out the exposure settings, the organisms used, and their strengths. The exposure method follows, together with the control samples needed to separate ultraviolet damage from handling effects. Tables compare fungal strengths and record the effect of the ultraviolet radiation on bacteria and on actinomycetes, a threadlike group of microbes. Results and a discussion close the study.
nasa-tm-19690008483-thermal-and-dielectr:
Ted A. Calvert of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report, TM X-1734, on the thermal and dielectric properties of a homogeneous Moon. His model treats the Moon as one uniform material throughout. He then tests that simple Moon against real microwave and infrared temperature observations gathered from Earth.

Early chapters build a heat flow model and fit smooth curves to the Moon's infrared surface temperatures. General microwave theory follows, with the links between heat traits and electrical traits worked out. Calvert then presents the experimental data and tests how well the uniform model matches it. Charts compare electrical conductivity against heat spread for separate sets of infrared data.
nasa-tm-19700017862-a-stress-corrosion-e:
J. W. Montano of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this evaluation on April 2, 1970. It tests AISI H-11 alloy steel that carries a nickel-cadmium plate. The question is how well the plated steel resists stress corrosion cracking.

Stress corrosion can crack a loaded metal part with little warning. A plate layer is meant to shield the steel, but the plate itself must hold up. Montano's tests judge the coated steel under stress in harsh settings. Builders of rockets and aircraft used such results to decide if the steel and plate could be trusted in service.
nasa-tm-19700033457-probability-learning:
Edward M. Huff of the Ames Research Center in California wrote this report in September 1970. It studies probability learning, how people learn to choose when outcomes are matters of chance. His claim is named in the title, the shortest path hypothesis, about which option a learner comes to favor.

Six groups of subjects faced different chance sequences that required predicting future events. In each sequence, the paths back to the preceding event varied in length from option to option. Huff predicted that subjects would favor the alternatives with the shortest such paths. The results, he reports, clearly support that prediction, and show how the shape of a chance environment steers human performance.
nasa-tm-19720008294-multiple-orifice-liq:
William L Weaver reported these hypersonic injection tests in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2486. Jets of liquid were sprayed sideways into air flowing at hypersonic speed. The nozzles had many small holes and sat on a flat plate. A cone shaped model, scaled from the RAM C spacecraft, carried side nozzles too. The work supported the RAM C-3 flight experiment. Injected liquid can cool or shield a craft's surface.

Water served as the safe test liquid. Three fluorocarbon liquids with special electrical traits were also sprayed. The data show how each spray spread and mixed in the fast stream. An errata sheet issued later corrects several photo pages. Weaver's results guided the design of the flight injection system.
nasa-tm-19720009526-experimental-evaluat:
Heinz L Wimmer of the Lewis Research Center evaluated this control circuit in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2502. The circuit served the isotope Brayton power system. In a Brayton system, an overload drags the spinning speed down fast. If voltage falls in step with speed, output power drops much faster still. That steep drop makes the system forgive overloads. Wimmer built a volts per hertz reference circuit to enforce that link.

The reference ties the voltage command to the frequency of the alternator. As frequency sags, the allowed voltage sags with it. Loads then draw less power, and the machine can recover. The report presents the bench evaluation of the circuit. Such protection helped small space power systems ride out faults safely.
seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-volume:
Francis W. Halsey edited this fifth volume of his travel set in 1914, opening Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Switzerland in Part One. A Berlin panorama from the town hall tower serves as the front picture. The tourist's routes run through Bremen and Hamburg, or by Antwerp and Rotterdam, with fast trains inland.

Famed writers describe cities, rivers, and mountain ground across the German lands and the Austrian empire. Swiss routes close the survey. Readers planning a grand tour got routes, scenes, and history in one place, drawn from writers who had walked the ground before them.

Francis W. Halsey edited this sixth volume of his travel set, carrying Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Switzerland into Part Two. Contents move from Hungary to Austria's Adriatic ports, then on to Alpine resorts. H. Tornai de Kover writes on Hungarian baths and on the Gypsies.

Edward A. Freeman guides readers through Trieste, Pola, Spalato, and Cattaro on the coast. Other stops include Cracow, Prague's road, the cave of Adelsberg, and the monastery of Molk. William Cullen Bryant crosses the Tyrol in these pages. The volume rounds out the empire's far corners for the armchair traveler.
stories-about-the-instinct-of-animals-th:
Thomas Bingley wrote Stories About the Instinct of Animals, Their Characters, and Habits, printed at New York and Boston in 1851 with engravings from drawings by T. Landseer. A storyteller called Uncle Thomas carries the book, telling tale after tale to young listeners.

The first chapter praises the horse: the vast herds on the plains of South America, their capture by lasso, the Arab and his mare, and stories of clever, loving, and tame horses. The beaver and its dam-building follow. Each chapter mixes real habits with striking anecdotes, so readers learn how animals act while enjoying the surprises of what they can do.
the-bradys-and-the-girl-smuggler-or-work:
The Bradys and the Girl Smuggler, or Working for the Custom House, ran as number 79 of the Secret Service weekly. Frank Tousey of New York put it out on July 27, 1900, at five cents a copy. The byline is A New York Detective. Its heroes are Old and Young King Brady, detectives now at work for the Custom House.

The tale opens in the office of the Collector of the Port of New York. He scores his chief inspectors for poor work and vows to stop the vast smuggling trade. If his own well-paid men can't do the work, he'll get some one who can. A plate shows Old King Brady serving a warrant on a lady for her daughter's arrest on a smuggling charge.
the-surprising-adventures-of-the-magical:
L. Frank Baum wrote these nonsense tales for children in 1903, with pictures by Frank Ver Beck, dedicating the book to the comrade of his boyhood days, Dr. Henry Clay Baum. His letter to the reader is dated June 1903. It confesses without shame a secret. The man who wrote it is also a child. His eyes still grow big at tales of the marvelous. His heart goes pit-a-pat at impossible adventures.

The stories are not true, Baum warns happily. They could not be true and be so marvelous. Nobody is expected to believe them. Their aim was laughter and a glad heart. Grown-ups who are still children will be comrades in the Magical Monarch's domain, while the others, self-exiled from it, need not be considered at all.
